item.title: Macuata set to host
item.description: THE Macuata Rugby Union women’s team will finally host its games in the Subrails Marama Cup Championship after six rounds of competition on Viti Levu. The Vanua Levu side has spent the opening rounds playing away from home but will now have the opportunity to compete in front of its supporters.
item.content:encoded:
THE Macuata Rugby Union women’s team will finally host its games in the Subrails Marama Cup Championship after six rounds of competition on Viti Levu.

The Vanua Levu side has spent the opening rounds playing away from home but will now have the opportunity to compete in front of its supporters.

Speaking to Times Sports last Saturday, Macuata head coach Motu Lalagavesi said the team was overjoyed and pleased with its progress and was looking forward to returning home after spending more than a month on Viti Levu.

“We are so happy that we are finally going back to Vanua Levu,” Lalagavesi said.

The side has faced several challenges during the competition, including spending more than a month in Suva away from home and having limited support during its campaign.

Despite the difficulties, the team has remained committed to the competition and continued to push through each round.

“We have been through so much challenges as a team, but I’m thankful to my players for holding on.”

Lalagavesi said the players had made sacrifices by staying away from their families for an extended period.

The side’s latest outing ended in a 22-19 win over Naitasiri, after leading 10-7 at halftime.

Lalagavesi added the result was a positive reflection of the players’ commitment despite the challenges they had faced.

The team will now prepare to return to Vanua Levu, where it will host its remaining home fixtures.

Playing at home is expected to provide the team with much-needed support and motivation as Macuata looks to finish its campaign strongly.

The side will also continue working on areas such as its scrums before its next match.

Macuata will host its home game on Taveuni and will take on Rewa for this week’s round seven clash of the Subrails Marama Cup Championship.

item.title: Two fail drug tests at BOG
item.description: TWO players tested positive at the first day of the 2026 Extra Battle of the Giants tournament at Govind Park in Ba, marking a significant moment in Fiji Football Association’s efforts to uphold integrity in football. Fiji Football Association chief executive officer Mohammed Yusuf confirmed that out of the 24 players tested on the opening day, these two players returned positive results.
item.content:encoded:
TWO players tested positive at the first day of the 2026 Extra Battle of the Giants tournament at Govind Park in Ba, marking a significant moment in Fiji Football Association’s efforts to uphold integrity in football.

Fiji Football Association chief executive officer Mohammed Yusuf confirmed that out of the 24 players tested on the opening day, these two players returned positive results.

“We concluded tests on day one with 24 tested. Unfortunately, two players tested positive,” Yusuf said.

The two players will now face the Fiji FA disciplinary committee as part of the next steps in the process.

“So, the process is they will appear before our disciplinary committee,” Yusuf explained.

Drug testing continued over the next two days, with 24 players tested each day, but no further positive results were recorded.

In total, 72 players underwent testing during the three-day opening phase of the tournament.

The drug testing initiative is part of Fiji FA’s commitment to ensuring accountability and fair play in the sport.

The tournament resumes this Saturday with the semi-finals, as Nasinu FC faces Rewa FC, and hosts Dayals Steels Ba FC take on Global Care Suva FC for a spot in the final.

item.title: Narayan’s rise from KajiKaji to Kulas

item.content:encoded:
THE final kick of Fiji’s 11-0 demolition of the Cook Islands belonged to Elisha Narayan. For the young Rewa defender, it was more than the last goal of a record victory. It was another step in a journey that began in grassroots football and has now taken her to the international stage.

Narayan joined Rewa Football Club’s Extra Red KajiKaji program in 2022. Four years on, the Nakasi High School student has progressed through the Delta Tigers’ under-16, U19 and senior women’s teams and into the Fiji U16 squad.

She marked her international tournament debut with a goal. Introduced from the bench, Narayan completed Fiji’s 11-0 win with the final kick of the game in Honiara.

The result was Fiji’s biggest victory at the OFC U16 Women’s Championship. But for Junior Kulas coach Nicola Demaine, there was little time for celebration.

Demaine praised the performance but urged her players to remain focused on the matches ahead. That is the reality of international football. For Narayan, it is also the next stage of an education that began at home.

Her development is a snapshot of what Fiji’s women’s football pathway can produce when grassroots, school and club football connect. She started with KajiKaji. Rewa provided the next platform.

School football gave her another avenue to compete and develop. The reward has been a place in the national team.

That progression matters because young female players need more than encouragement to stay in football. They need opportunities to play, coaches to develop them and competitions that allow them to test themselves as they move through the age groups. Narayan has benefited from that progression.

Now she is becoming an example for those following behind her.

Her story tells the young girl playing football on a school field that the Fiji jersey is not an impossible dream. The journey can start locally.

The next challenge is ensuring more players are given the same opportunity. For the Junior Kulas, the stakes in Honiara are high.

The top two teams will qualify for the 2027 FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco. Narayan is therefore not simply part of Fiji’s present.

She represents an investment in its future. Her goal against the Cook Islands may have come with the final kick of the match.

Her football journey, however, is only beginning. From Red KajiKaji to Rewa. From Rewa to Fiji. Narayan’s rise is proof that when the pathway is there, young Fijian girls can take it.

item.title: FORMER 7s STAR EMBRACEs FLYING FIJIANS OPPORTUNITY
item.description: FIJI Water Flying Fijians new squad member Terio Tamani says he is embracing the opportunity to represent Fiji in the 15-man code as the national side prepares to defend its Pacific Nations Cup title this year. Nicknamed ‘Terrific’ Tamani by World Rugby 7s commentators, the former Fiji 7s player says the transition from sevens to fifteens has been one of the biggest challenges of his rugby journey
item.content:encoded:
FIJI Water Flying Fijians new squad member Terio Tamani says he is embracing the opportunity to represent Fiji in the 15-man code as the national side prepares to defend its Pacific Nations Cup title this year.

Nicknamed ‘Terrific’ Tamani by World Rugby 7s commentators, the former Fiji 7s player says the transition from sevens to fifteens has been one of the biggest challenges of his rugby journey.

Tamani first thanked God for the opportunity to join the national team and wear the Fiji jersey.

“Firstly, I thank the Lord for the opportunity to join the Flying Fijians and don the 15s national jersey,” Tamani said.

“Training and preparation for the upcoming Pacific Nations Cup has been going well, especially the transition from 7s rugby to 15s. There is more structure to learn, and it has been good.”

Tamani said his involvement with the Kadavu senior men’s team in this year’s Skipper Cup competition had also helped him build momentum and reconnect with his roots in the 15-man game.

“I think it’s a good start, going back to my roots of playing for the Kadavu senior men’s Skipper Cup team this year,” he said.

“I’m thankful to be called up and to be joining the brothers in the Flying Fijians.”

The call-up, however, came as a surprise to the talented halfback, who admitted he never expected to be selected for the national squad.

“Firstly, I didn’t believe that I’d be called up to join the squad,” he said.

“It has been a big challenge for me, especially the transition from 7s to 15s. There is more structure and we have to work hard to beat our opponents, especially for us halfbacks.”

With Fiji looking to successfully defend its Pacific Nations Cup crown, Tamani said he would focus on fulfilling his responsibilities and ensuring quality service from the base of the scrum.

“I’ll just focus on my job, delivering every play and quality passes to the forwards, and making sure there is a good connection from the forwards to the backline,” he said.

Tamani has also enjoyed reuniting with several former Fiji 7s teammates, including Joji Nasova, while learning from experienced Flying Fijians halfback Frank Lomani.

“I have learnt a lot from the backline, especially from Frank Lomani and the other players,” Tamani said.

“It has been so good to come and play again with my former 7s teammates.”

The 2026 World Rugby Pacific Nations Cup starts in Japan this Saturday.

Fiji plays Canada in the first semi-final at 7pm at Hanazono Rugby Stadium, Higashiosaka City, Osaka Prefecture.

Fiji Water Flying Fijians player Terio Tamani trains at the Drua Gym in Nadi on 3rd September 2026. Picture: REINAL CHAND

item.title: A step up for Rawaqa
item.description: THE appointment of former Flying Fijian forward Ifereimi Rawaqa as forwards coach of the Swire Shipping Fijian Drua could prove to be as important for Fiji’s coaches as it is for the franchise’s forward pack. Rawaqa’s elevation is being viewed by the Fiji Rugby Union as a significant step in its push to establish a structured pathway for local coaches to progress into the professional and internat
item.content:encoded:
THE appointment of former Flying Fijian forward Ifereimi Rawaqa as forwards coach of the Swire Shipping Fijian Drua could prove to be as important for Fiji’s coaches as it is for the franchise’s forward pack.

Rawaqa’s elevation is being viewed by the Fiji Rugby Union as a significant step in its push to establish a structured pathway for local coaches to progress into the professional and international game.

FRU chief executive officer Koli Sewabu said the appointment was part of a wider alignment strategy between the union and the Drua, which was designed to develop not only players but also coaches and management personnel.

“On behalf of Fiji Rugby, I just wanted to acknowledge and thank Drua CEO Mark Evans, the coaches and the management team for their belief and their support in our coach development pathway,” Sewabu said.

“Especially for the appointment of Ifereimi and Campese Ma’afu (scrum coach) into the Drua set-up.”

For Rawaqa, the opportunity represents the progression of a coaching journey that has already taken him through the Fiji Warriors and the Drua development system.

But what makes his appointment significant is what he brings into the position.

A former Flying Fijian, Rawaqa has first-hand experience of international rugby and the demands placed on Fiji’s forwards at the highest level.

That combination could prove valuable to a Drua side that continues to develop players from Fiji’s provincial and grassroots competitions into Super Rugby Pacific professionals.

As a coach, Rawaqa has been exposed to player development and high-performance environments, giving him an understanding of the transition required from raw Fijian talent to professional rugby.

His appointment also gives the Drua a local coach who understands the cultural and rugby context from which many of its players come.

Sewabu believes that is precisely what the Drua was created to facilitate.

“This is an alignment strategy and alignment piece that we’re working on and really showcases what Drua is originally built for — not only a pathway for our players but also a pathway for our coaches, our management,” he said.

That pathway, however, will only work if FRU and the Drua operate with a common purpose.

FRU owns a minority share of the Fijian Drua, making the relationship between the governing body and the professional franchise critical to Fiji’s long-term rugby development.

The Drua cannot simply be viewed as a Super Rugby team, while FRU cannot operate its development programmes separately from the country’s professional pathway.

The two must work cordially, share knowledge and align their systems so the pathway becomes seamless — from local rugby to the Drua and ultimately the Flying Fijians.

Sewabu said the union was working to ensure systems were put in place to support coaches as they progressed through the elite pathway.

But he also placed responsibility on the coaches themselves.

“It’s also important from a Fiji Rugby perspective that our coaches commit to their own personal and professional development growth,” he said.

“The system is here to provide them with further assistance when they start to go up the elite pathways.”

item.title: Bower out to make a statement
item.description: GEORGE Bower has been given the All Blacks chance he has spent years waiting for. The Fiji-born prop is in line to feature in Saturday’s final Test against South Africa in Baltimore, where New Zealand will attempt to finish the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series on level terms.
item.content:encoded:
GEORGE Bower has been given the All Blacks chance he has spent years waiting for.

The Fiji-born prop is in line to feature in Saturday’s final Test against South Africa in Baltimore, where New Zealand will attempt to finish the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series on level terms.

For Bower, this is more than another Test against the Springboks.

It is an opportunity to turn a long history of being overlooked into a compelling case for a permanent place in the All Blacks picture.

The 34-year-old has already taken significant steps during this series, featuring in all three Tests and progressing from the bench to the starting XV.

It suggests Dave Rennie is beginning to see Bower not simply as experienced cover, but as a prop capable of confronting the most demanding forward pack in world rugby.

He knows the physical language of South African rugby.

He understands that against the Springboks there are no hiding places for a front-rower.

The scrum is a battlefield, every carry is a collision, and every defensive effort demands accuracy.

Bower brings experience, strength and a growing ability to contribute beyond the set-piece.

item.title: World Cup hope ends for Fiji U19 but team will continue fighting
item.description: FIJI’s hopes of qualifying for the 2027 FIFA Under-20 World Cup have ended after a 2-1 loss to Tahiti, but midfielder Nicholas Franklin says the team will continue to fight until the end of its campaign. Franklin said Fiji started the match well and had control of the game early but struggled to maintain its momentum as Tahiti took charge.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’s hopes of qualifying for the 2027 FIFA Under-20 World Cup have ended after a 2-1 loss to Tahiti, but midfielder Nicholas Franklin says the team will continue to fight until the end of its campaign.

Franklin said Fiji started the match well and had control of the game early but struggled to maintain its momentum as Tahiti took charge.

“It was a tough one. Tahiti played really well,” Franklin said.

“At the start we had control of the game, but we sort of lost it throughout, and that was a big decider for us.”

Despite the disappointment, Franklin praised his teammates for their effort throughout the match.

“The boys fought to the last minute, which is all that matters for us – to be at the end and fight to the end,” he said.

Franklin acknowledged that Tahiti were the better side on the day but said there was no time to dwell on the defeat with one match remaining.

He said the players would lift their heads and remain focused on representing Fiji.

“We’re still playing for our country. We still want to do us proud, so to the end we’ll fight and hopefully give them a good result the next time,” Franklin said.

Fiji’s World Cup qualification hopes are now over, but Franklin said the team would look to finish the campaign on a positive note.

He also apologised to supporters back home for the result and promised the players would continue fighting for a win in their final match.

item.title: Support for former players
item.description: FOUR former football players will receive financial assistance as part of the 2026 RC Manubhai/Apco Coatings Veterans Tournament this weekend. The Fiji Football Association will present $500 education vouchers to each of the four deserving former players before the first Extra Battle of the Giants semi-final between Suva and Ba.
item.content:encoded:
FOUR former football players will receive financial assistance as part of the 2026 RC Manubhai/Apco Coatings Veterans Tournament this weekend.

The Fiji Football Association will present $500 education vouchers to each of the four deserving former players before the first Extra Battle of the Giants semi-final between Suva and Ba.

Fiji Football Association chief executive officer Mohammed Yusuf said the initiative was part of the association’s commitment to supporting former players beyond their playing days.

He said the veteran’s tournament was not organised for profit, with sponsorship and registration fees channelled back into the welfare and wellbeing of the former players.

“This year again Abdul Mananan and his team will be identifying four very deserving former players who need some financial assistance for their children’s educational needs,” Yusuf said.

Yusuf said the association had provided the $500 vouchers to four veterans annually for the past seven years.

The initiative has been supported by RC Manubhai and Apco Coatings, which have been involved with the veteran’s tournament since it began 12 years ago.Yusuf acknowledged the companies for their continued contribution towards supporting former players and their families.

He said the assistance was particularly important for veterans who had limited means to support the education of their children or grandchildren.

The RC Manubhai/Apco Coatings Veterans Tournament will be held this weekend alongside the BOG program.
